title: What My Mentor Taught Me About Receiving Criticism Well
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] For years, I believed that receiving criticism gracefully simply meant nodding politely while secretly disagreeing with every single word.
Narrator: Whenever my mentor reviewed my writing, I would thank her out loud while quietly building a defense in my head at the same time.
Narrator: [carefully] I assumed that was normal, even necessary, as though feedback were something to survive rather than something worth genuinely absorbing.
Narrator: Then, last spring, she said something during a review that completely changed how I understood the entire process.
Narrator: [reflective] She told me, if you're only listening to decide how you'll defend yourself, you're not actually listening at all, you're merely waiting.
Narrator: That sentence stung, mostly because it was accurate, and I had never noticed the pattern in myself until she named it directly.
Narrator: [honestly] I started paying closer attention after that, and I noticed how quickly my mind jumped to justification whenever anyone questioned my work.
Narrator: So I began practicing something uncomfortable. Before responding to criticism, I now force myself to repeat the person's point back to them first.
Narrator: [seriously] Not to agree automatically, but simply to prove I had genuinely understood what they meant, rather than what I assumed they meant.
Narrator: It felt awkward at first, almost robotic, and a few colleagues even asked why I kept repeating their sentences back so carefully.
Narrator: [gently] However, something shifted once I made this a habit. People started offering more honest feedback, since they trusted I would actually hear it.
Narrator: I also learned that receiving criticism well doesn't mean accepting every point automatically, despite what I once assumed about politeness.
Narrator: [encouraging] Sometimes, after truly listening, I still disagree, and I say so calmly, once I'm certain I've understood their concern completely.
Narrator: My mentor calls this the difference between hearing and defending, and I think about that distinction almost every single week now.

quiz.question: How did the narrator used to handle criticism from her mentor?
options: She thanked her mentor while secretly building a defense in her head
She always argued out loud immediately
She stopped meeting with her mentor
quiz.explanation: She would thank her mentor out loud while quietly preparing a defense in her mind.

quiz.question: What did her mentor say that changed her perspective?
options: That her writing needed no improvement
That criticism should always be ignored
That only waiting to defend yourself isn't actually listening
quiz.explanation: Her mentor said that only listening to prepare a defense means you're not really listening, just waiting.

quiz.question: What new habit did the narrator start practicing?
options: Repeating the person's point back before responding
Asking someone else to receive feedback for her
quiz.explanation: She began repeating the other person's point back to prove she truly understood it before responding.

quiz.question: How did colleagues react to this new habit at first?
options: They asked why she kept repeating their sentences so carefully
quiz.explanation: A few colleagues asked why she kept repeating their sentences back so carefully, since it felt unusual at first.

quiz.question: Does the narrator believe receiving criticism well means agreeing with everything?
options: No, she can still disagree calmly once she's understood the concern
No, she should never respond at all
Yes, but only with close friends
quiz.explanation: She clarifies that receiving criticism well doesn't mean automatic agreement; she can disagree calmly after truly understanding the point.

quiz.question: What makes feedback usable?
options: Specific examples, expected standard, evidence, and a chance to clarify

quiz.question: Why might repeating a point be unsafe?
options: Power imbalance or hostile feedback may require documentation and another channel

quiz.question: What can the narrator do after understanding?
options: Ask questions, provide evidence, disagree, or use review routes

quiz.question: What must a mentor avoid?
options: Humiliation, discrimination, harassment, retaliation, or false certainty

quiz.question: What distinguishes hearing from defending?
options: Understanding a concern before choosing how to respond
